summary: This document updates the RSVP-TE Fast Reroute procedures in RFC 4090 so they work for packet-switch-capable GMPLS label switched paths. The updates allow a bidirectional bypass tunnel to be coordinated, so protection works in both directions.

eli5.summary: If a road is closed, a detour is set up for traffic going both ways, and both ends agree on it.

questions: how does fast reroute work with gmpls
what is a point of remote repair
subtitle: Makes MPLS fast reroute work for two-way GMPLS paths, so both directions switch to the same detour.

tldr.problem: When fast reroute protects a co-routed bidirectional GMPLS path, the two directions can pick different detours, and RSVP refreshes can stop reaching some nodes so the path times out and is torn down.
tldr.mechanism: A new BYPASS_ASSIGNMENT subobject in the Path RRO tells the upstream node which bypass tunnel was chosen, and a downstream merge point is promoted to a Point of Remote Repair that moves the reverse direction onto the same bypass tunnel.
tldr.outcome: Traffic and signaling flow over co-routed paths after the reroute and the protected path survives RSVP soft-state timeout. The RFC updates RFC 4090.

today: RFC 8271 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4090. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem with Two-Way Protected Paths
sections.content:
Packet Switch Capable (PSC) Traffic Engineering label switched paths (LSPs) can be set up with GMPLS signaling (RFC 3473) as unidirectional or bidirectional tunnels. Fast Reroute (RFC 4090) is described as widely deployed in packet TE networks and is wanted for GMPLS LSPs too.

RFC 4090 describes how the Point of Local Repair (PLR) moves traffic and signaling onto a bypass tunnel. For co-routed bidirectional LSPs the same PLR and Merge Point pair should be chosen in each direction and both should assign the same bidirectional bypass tunnel.

There is a second problem. After a failure with node protection bypass tunnels, the upstream and downstream PLRs trigger reroute independently, so signaling may take asymmetric paths. RSVP refreshes can stop reaching certain nodes, and the RSVP soft-state timeout then tears down the LSP with traffic loss. The protection state coordination protocol of RFC 6378 does not address this control-plane timeout.

Unless stated otherwise, the procedures of RFC 4090 are unchanged. Associated bidirectional LSPs built from two unidirectional ones (RFC 7551) are out of scope.
sections.eli5: When a road closes you want the cars going each way to use the same detour, and you want the road signs on both ends to stay up to date.

sections.title: Roles in the Reroute
sections.content:
The RFC splits the usual roles by direction. A downstream PLR detects a failure in the direction of traffic flow and reroutes in the same direction as the RSVP Path signaling; its downstream Merge Point (MP) is where the backup tunnel rejoins the protected path. An upstream PLR reroutes in the opposite direction, and has a corresponding upstream MP. One router can be a downstream MP and an upstream PLR at once.

The document also defines the Point of Remote Repair (PRR): a downstream MP that, on receiving the rerouted Path message, takes the role of upstream PLR and triggers the reroute of traffic and signaling in the upstream direction.
sections.eli5: Each end of a detour has a name: the spot where traffic leaves the road and the spot where it rejoins. The new job is a helper who makes the other direction follow the same detour.

sections.title: Coordinating the Bypass Tunnel
sections.content:
Bidirectional bypass tunnels are signaled in the same direction as the protected LSP, so the downstream PLR, which knows its local policy, always starts the assignment. Upstream and downstream PLRs learn merge point labels and addresses from the RRO (Record Route Object) as in RFC 4090 and RFC 4561.

When these procedures are used, each downstream PLR MUST add a BYPASS_ASSIGNMENT subobject to the Path RRO of the protected LSP. It goes immediately after the Node-ID address, which MUST match the source address of the chosen bypass tunnel, and a Label subobject MUST also be added. The upstream PLR (the downstream MP) simply reflects the assignment in the reverse direction. If the subobject is absent, that node or interface is not protected by a bidirectional bypass tunnel.

If the upstream PLR cannot find the tunnel it SHOULD send a Notify message, and the downstream PLR then SHOULD remove the assignment and pick another tunnel if one is available. With one-to-one backup, a bypass tunnel already in use triggers a similar error. When several downstream PLRs send assignments, for example one for node protection and one for link protection, the upstream PLR SHOULD report that it cannot use the assignment. The asymmetry can be avoided using the node protection desired flag in the SESSION_ATTRIBUTE object.
sections.eli5: Before anything breaks, the router at one end writes down which detour it plans to use. The router at the other end reads the note and plans for the same detour, and complains if it cannot.

sections.title: What Happens After a Failure
sections.content:
With in-band signaling, the downstream PLR reroutes traffic and Path messages onto the bypass tunnel. The upstream PLR reroutes traffic when it sees the link fail or receives a Path message over the bypass tunnel, and then reroutes Resv messages. Traffic and signaling thus use symmetric paths.

For link protection (R3-R4 fails in the RFC's example), R3 and R4 independently move traffic onto bypass tunnel T3, and R4 reroutes Resv after receiving the Path message over T3. For node protection there are two phases: first fast reroute of data in both directions, then restoring co-routing of signaling and data. After the first phase R4 stops getting Path refreshes and does not reroute Resv.

In the second phase the downstream MP (R5) that receives the rerouted Path message becomes the PRR. It finds the reverse bypass tunnel ending at the downstream PLR, using the tunnel sender address in the SENDER_TEMPLATE object, and moves traffic and Resv onto it. If no reverse tunnel is found, the PRR immediately tears down the protected LSP. R4 then times out its RSVP soft state, but this does not tear the LSP down. With several failures, the PRR picks the tunnel ending at the farthest downstream PLR.

Revertive behavior from RFC 4090 still applies after the link is restored. Unidirectional failures in the upstream direction can cause soft-state timeout at the downstream PLR with in-band signaling, whereas out-of-band signaling avoids this.
sections.eli5: When a road breaks, each side first rushes cars onto its own detour. Then a helper makes sure the road signs and the cars all end up on one shared detour, and the old broken stretch is forgotten.

sections.title: The BYPASS_ASSIGNMENT Subobject
sections.content:
The subobject informs the downstream MP of the bypass tunnel the PLR assigned. It SHOULD be inserted into the Path RRO by the downstream PLR, SHOULD NOT be inserted by a node that is not a downstream PLR, MUST NOT be changed by downstream LSRs and MUST NOT be added to a Resv RRO.

The IPv4 form has type 38 and a length of 8 bytes: a 16-bit Bypass Tunnel ID and the bypass tunnel IPv4 destination address. The IPv6 form has type 39 and a length of 20 bytes, with a 16-byte destination address.

The RFC also defines Error Code 44, FRR Bypass Assignment Error, carried in a Notify message sent by the upstream PLR to the downstream PLR. It MUST NOT be sent in a Path Error message and does not cause the protected LSP to be torn down.
sections.eli5: It is a small note stuck on the message that says which detour tunnel to use and where it ends.

sections.title: Compatibility and Security
sections.content:
Nodes that do not support the new subobject ignore it but forward it unmodified (RFC 3209), and nodes that do not support the new Notify error ignore it and forward it without modification.

The subobject lets an eavesdropper deduce more about an LSP's fast reroute protection. The RFC judges this a very minor risk since the information is available by other means. An MP that finds no matching bypass tunnel ignores the subobject, so inserting a random address is also minimal risk. The error does not tear down the LSP. A PLR and its merge point trust RSVP messages from each other, as in RFC 4090, and the security considerations of RSVP-TE and GMPLS (RFC 3209, RFC 3473) still apply.
sections.eli5: Old routers just pass the note along without reading it, and the note reveals only a little that spies could already find out.
